args.text: [lane-wren] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System, the internet's address book) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: a site moves to a new server, but users are still sent to the old one, so pages fail or show outdated content. (2) Slow recovery: if a service fails over to a backup address, cached answers delay the switch, prolonging the outage. (3) Lingering bad answers: a poisoned or hijacked record stays in the cache and keeps misdirecting users long after the problem is fixed.

[lane-wren] Idempotent (safe to repeat) retries matter because networks fail unpredictably, so a sender often cannot tell whether its first request was actioned. If repeating a request has the same effect as sending it once, the sender can retry freely without causing duplicates, such as a customer being charged twice.

[lane-wren] Two trade-offs of UUIDv7 (a universally unique identifier that begins with a timestamp) as a primary key: (1) Leaks timing: the ID reveals roughly when a row was created, which may expose business activity or help guessing neighbouring IDs. (2) Size: at 16 bytes it is larger than a typical whole-number key, so indexes take more space, though its time ordering keeps inserts far friendlier than random UUIDs.

[lane-wren] A write-ahead log (WAL) is a record that a database writes to disk describing each change before it applies that change to the main data files. If the system crashes, it replays this log to recover finished work and undo unfinished work, so no confirmed change is lost and the data stays consistent.

[lane-wren] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Fair comparison: if the client software changes between runs, any speed difference might come from the client rather than the system being tested. (2) Repeatability: others can rerun the test later and get comparable results, because behaviour, defaults and bug fixes in newer client versions can change the numbers.
